answer:
# NRC dose limits for individual members of the public

Governing provision: **10 CFR Part 20, Subpart D (Radiation Dose Limits for Individual Members of the Public)**, Sec. 20.1301, with the compliance provision at Sec. 20.1302. Text below is quoted verbatim from the eCFR current text and the GovInfo CFR-2025 print (both fetched 2026-11-15; the two agree word-for-word).

## 1. The two limits asked for

| # | Context | Limit | SI equivalent | Citation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | Annual, individual member of the public, total effective dose equivalent (TEDE) from the licensed operation | **0.1 rem in a year** | 1 mSv in a year | Sec. 20.1301(a)(1) |
| B | **Any one hour**, unrestricted area, from **external sources** | **0.002 rem in any one hour** | 0.02 mSv in any one hour (0.02 mSv/h) | Sec. 20.1301(a)(2) |

Ask 1 of the request is limit B: **0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in any one hour in an unrestricted area.**

## 2. Verbatim regulatory text (Sec. 20.1301)

> Sec. 20.1301 Dose limits for individual members of the public.
>
> (a) Each licensee shall conduct operations so that-
>
> (1) The total effective dose equivalent to individual members of the public from the licensed operation does not exceed 0.1 rem (1 mSv) in a year, exclusive of the dose contributions from background radiation, from any medical administration the individual has received, from exposure to individuals administered radioactive material and released under Sec. 35.75, from voluntary participation in medical research programs, and from the licensee's disposal of radioactive material into sanitary sewerage in accordance with Sec. 20.2003, and
>
> (2) The dose in any unrestricted area from external sources, exclusive of the dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with Sec. 35.75, does not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 millisievert) in any one hour.
>
> (b) If the licensee permits members of the public to have access to controlled areas, the limits for members of the public continue to apply to those individuals.
>
> (c) Notwithstanding paragraph (a)(1) of this section, a licensee may permit visitors to an individual who cannot be released, under Sec. 35.75, to receive a radiation dose greater than 0.1 rem (1 mSv) if-
>
> (1) The radiation dose received does not exceed 0.5 rem (5 mSv); and
>
> (2) The authorized user, as defined in 10 CFR Part 35, has determined before the visit that it is appropriate.
>
> (d) A licensee or license applicant may apply for prior NRC authorization to operate up to an annual dose limit for an individual member of the public of 0.5 rem (5 mSv). The licensee or license applicant shall include the following information in this application:
>
> (1) Demonstration of the need for and the expected duration of operations in excess of the limit in paragraph (a) of this section;
>
> (2) The licensee's program to assess and control dose within the 0.5 rem (5 mSv) annual limit; and
>
> (3) The procedures to be followed to maintain the dose as low as is reasonably achievable.
>
> (e) In addition to the requirements of this part, a licensee subject to the provisions of EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in 40 CFR part 190 shall comply with those standards.
>
> (f) The Commission may impose additional restrictions on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on the total quantity of radionuclides that a licensee may release in effluents in order to restrict the collective dose.

## 3. What each limit actually covers (the fine print that changes the number)

**Limit A - annual, 0.1 rem (1 mSv) TEDE.**
- Quantity is **total effective dose equivalent**, i.e. the sum of the deep-dose equivalent from external exposure plus the committed effective dose equivalent from internal (inhalation/ingestion) uptake. It is not a whole-body-only or external-only figure.
- It is measured **per individual member of the public**, at the individual likely to receive the highest dose (the "maximally exposed individual"), not an average over a population.
- It attaches to dose **from the licensed operation** only. The regulation expressly **excludes**: background radiation; medical administration the individual has received; exposure to patients released under Sec. 35.75; voluntary participation in medical research programs; and the licensee's disposal of radioactive material to sanitary sewerage under Sec. 20.2003. Those contributions are not counted against the 0.1 rem.
- Applies in **a year** - i.e. it is a cumulative 12-month quantity, not an instantaneous rate.

**Limit B - hourly, 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv).**
- Quantity is **dose from external sources only**. There is no internal/inhalation component in the hourly limit; internal exposure is controlled separately through the effluent concentration limits of appendix B, table 2 (see Sec. 20.1302(b)(2)(i) below).
- Location is **any unrestricted area** - the limit applies at every point in the unrestricted area, not only at a single designated boundary marker.
- Time base is **any one hour** - the highest one-hour dose anywhere in the unrestricted area at any time. It is not a daily, monthly or annual average, and there is no occupancy factor applied: a location that is occupied zero hours per year must still satisfy it.
- Sole exclusion: dose contributions from patients administered radioactive material and released in accordance with Sec. 35.75.
- Sec. 20.1301(b): if the licensee lets members of the public into controlled areas, these public limits continue to apply to those individuals while they are there.

**Definitional note (not in the fetched source set - verify before citing):** 10 CFR 20.1003 defines "unrestricted area" essentially as an area to which access is neither limited nor controlled by the licensee, and defines "member of the public" as any individual other than one receiving an occupational dose. The exact wording of Sec. 20.1003 was not among the retrieved passages, so it is paraphrased here and should be quoted from the current eCFR before it goes into a licensing document.

## 4. Exceptions and ceilings that sit above the 0.1 rem

These are **not** the general public limit; they are narrow, conditional relaxations, and stating 0.5 rem as "the" limit would be wrong.

1. **Visitor exception, Sec. 20.1301(c).** A licensee may permit visitors to an individual who cannot be released under Sec. 35.75 to exceed 0.1 rem, provided the visitor's dose does not exceed **0.5 rem (5 mSv)** and the authorized user determined beforehand that the visit is appropriate. This is a medical-patient-visitation provision, not an operating margin.
2. **Authorized alternative annual limit, Sec. 20.1301(d).** A licensee or applicant may apply for **prior NRC authorization** to operate up to **0.5 rem (5 mSv)** per year for an individual member of the public, submitting (i) the need and expected duration of operation above 0.1 rem, (ii) the program to assess and control dose within the 0.5 rem limit, and (iii) procedures to keep dose ALARA. Absent that written authorization, 0.1 rem/y is the limit.
3. **EPA standards, Sec. 20.1301(e).** A licensee subject to EPA's generally applicable environmental radiation standards in **40 CFR part 190** must also comply with those standards; they can be more restrictive than 0.1 rem/y and then govern. (Note: the numeric values in 40 CFR 190 were not in the retrieved sources and are not stated here - pull them from the current CFR before relying on them.)
4. **Commission-imposed restrictions, Sec. 20.1301(f).** The Commission may impose additional limits on radiation levels in unrestricted areas and on quantities released, to restrict collective dose. License conditions and technical specifications can therefore be stricter than Part 20.
5. **ALARA.** Separately from the numeric limits, licensees must keep doses as low as reasonably achievable (10 CFR 20.1101); compliance with 0.1 rem/y is not by itself a defense. (Paraphrase - not in the fetched source set.)

## 5. How compliance with each limit is demonstrated (Sec. 20.1302, verbatim)

> Sec. 20.1302 Compliance with dose limits for individual members of the public.
>
> (a) The licensee shall make or cause to be made, as appropriate, surveys of radiation levels in unrestricted and controlled areas and radioactive materials in effluents released to unrestricted and controlled areas to demonstrate compliance with the dose limits for individual members of the public in Sec. 20.1301.
>
> (b) A licensee shall show compliance with the annual dose limit in Sec. 20.1301 by-
>
> (1) Demonstrating by measurement or calculation that the total effective dose equivalent to the individual likely to receive the highest dose from the licensed operation does not exceed the annual dose limit; or
>
> (2) Demonstrating that-
>
> (i) The annual average concentrations of radioactive material released in gaseous and liquid effluents at the boundary of the unrestricted area do not exceed the values specified in table 2 of appendix B to part 20; and
>
> (ii) If an individual were continuously present in an unrestricted area, the dose from external sources would not exceed 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) in an hour and 0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) in a year.
>
> (c) Upon approval from the Commission, the licensee may adjust the effluent concentration values in appendix B to part 20, table 2, for members of the public, to take into account the actual physical and chemical characteristics of the effluents (e.g., aerosol size distribution, solubility, density, radioactive decay equilibrium, chemical form).

Two things follow directly from Sec. 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) that matter to anyone implementing this:
- There is a **third number** in the public-dose scheme: **0.05 rem (0.5 mSv) per year from external sources**, evaluated on the assumption that an individual is **continuously present** in the unrestricted area. It is a compliance-demonstration criterion, not a separate Sec. 20.1301 limit, but it is enforceable through Sec. 20.1302 and is more restrictive than the 0.1 rem TEDE limit for the external pathway.
- The hourly 0.002 rem figure appears **twice** - once as the operative limit in Sec. 20.1301(a)(2) and once as the continuous-occupancy demonstration test in Sec. 20.1302(b)(2)(ii). Same number, both 0.002 rem (0.02 mSv) per hour.

## 6. Engineering consistency check on the numbers (do not skip this)

- Unit conversions used throughout: 1 rem = 10 mSv. Therefore 0.1 rem = 1 mSv; 0.002 rem = 0.02 mSv; 0.05 rem = 0.5 mSv; 0.5 rem = 5 mSv. Every metric value in this document is the regulation's own parenthetical conversion.
- **The hourly limit does not bound the annual limit.** At exactly 0.002 rem/h for a full year: 0.002 x 8760 = **17.52 rem/y**, which is 350.4 times the 0.05 rem/y external-source value in Sec. 20.1302(b)(2)(ii) and 175 times the 0.1 rem/y TEDE limit. A design that just meets the hourly limit at a continuously occupied point therefore fails the annual test by two orders of magnitude. The binding constraint for continuous occupancy is the **0.05 rem/y external** value, which corresponds to an average external rate of 0.05 / 8760 = **5.71 microrem/h (0.0571 microSv/h)** - about 1/350 of the 2 mrem/h ceiling.
- **No internal conflict between the 0.05 and 0.1 rem figures:** external dose is a component of TEDE, so an external cap of 0.05 rem/y is necessarily below the 0.1 rem/y TEDE cap. The 0.5 rem figures in Sec. 20.1301(c) and (d) sit above both and are reachable only through the stated conditions (authorized user determination; prior NRC authorization), so they do not contradict the 0.1 rem default.
- **Practical design targets:** set the boundary/offsite external dose-rate alarm and the survey action level at a small fraction of 2 mrem/h (e.g. an investigation level around 0.1-0.5 mrem/h) and the annual offsite external assessment at a small fraction of 50 mrem, so that ALARA margin exists and instrument uncertainty does not put a measured value on the limit itself. Instantaneous area monitors or dose-rate surveys demonstrate the hourly limit; boundary TLD/OSLD or environmental dosimetry plus effluent pathway calculation demonstrate the annual limit.
